explanations.explanation: Twelve it is, friend. Manasseh, Hezekiah's son, is twelve years old when he becomes king, and he reigns in Jerusalem fifty-five years. At twelve I couldn't have been trusted with a kitchen timer, and this young man gets a whole kingdom. That's a LOT of crown for a small head.

Eight is a real age for a king, but it isn't Manasseh's. Josiah, who is Amon's son and comes later in this passage, becomes king at eight (2 Chronicles 34:1). Manasseh is older than that when he starts. The verse says he was twelve.

Sixteen is a nice round number, friend, but the verse doesn't use it. Manasseh was twelve years old when he became king. So he's four years younger than your guess. That's a young king with a long road ahead of him.

Fifty-five years, friend! He reigns in Jerusalem longer than anyone would guess from a twelve-year-old with a crown. His father Hezekiah, the king before him, reigned twenty-nine years (2 Chronicles 29:1). So Manasseh nearly doubles his father's run. That's a lot of mornings on one throne.

Forty is a solid number, friend, and it sounds like a good long reign. But the verse says fifty-five years for Manasseh. He has fifteen more years than you gave him. That's a whole lot of extra throne time.

Twenty-nine is a real number in this family, friend. It's how long Manasseh's father Hezekiah reigned in Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 29:1). But Manasseh doesn't match his father here. His reign is fifty-five years.

Rebuilt, friend. His father Hezekiah tore the high places down, and Manasseh builds them right back up. That's like sweeping the whole counter spotless and then someone tips a tray of crumbs over it before you can put the broom down. One man does the cleanup and the next one undoes it.

Avoiding them would have been the opposite of what happens, friend. The verse says Manasseh rebuilt the high places his father Hezekiah had torn down. He doesn't stay away from them. He puts them back up.

Forgot makes it sound like they slipped his mind, friend, like a cookie sheet left on the counter. The verse is plainer than that. It says he rebuilt the high places that his father Hezekiah had torn down. Building takes work, so this is an action he takes.

True, friend. The verse says he raised up altars for the Baals and made Asherah poles, along with rebuilding the high places. The Baals and Asherah poles are the kind of worship that comes from the nations around Judah. Manasseh is stacking one wrong thing on top of another.
This one is True, friend. The verse says Manasseh raised up altars for the Baals and made Asherah poles. He did that along with rebuilding the high places. So the statement matches the text.

Both courtyards, friend. The verse says, “In both courtyards of the house of the LORD, he built altars to all the host of heaven.” That means these altars sit right inside the LORD's house, in two places. There's no corner of that place he leaves alone.
The rooftop is a good guess if you're picturing a high place, friend. But this verse never mentions a rooftop. It says he built the altars in both courtyards of the house of the LORD.
No storerooms in this verse, friend. The text puts these altars out in the open, in both courtyards of the house of the LORD. Nothing about hiding them in the back.

This one is False, friend. The verse says the opposite. Manasseh practiced sorcery, divination and witchcraft, and he consulted mediums and spiritists. I think this part is heavy, so let's just say it plainly and move on.

False is right, friend. Manasseh doesn't stay away from any of it. The verse says he practiced sorcery, divination and witchcraft, and consulted mediums and spiritists. It's a heavy part of the story, and the verse says it plainly.

explanations.answer: That they carefully do all He commanded through Moses
explanations.explanation: That's the condition, friend. God spoke to David, Israel's king, and his son Solomon, and said He would never again cause the Israelites to leave the land, “…if only they are careful to do all that I have commanded them through Moses…” The promise comes with a "carefully do" attached. Manasseh leads the people the other way.

explanations.answer: That they build Him a bigger and grander temple
explanations.explanation: A bigger temple isn't in the deal, friend. God told David, Israel's king, and his son Solomon that the Israelites would stay in the land if only they were careful to do all He commanded through Moses. The condition is about doing what He said. Nothing in the verse asks for a grander building.

explanations.answer: That they defeat every nation living around them
explanations.explanation: Defeating every nation sounds like a big job, friend, but it isn't what God asked. The condition He gave David, Israel's king, and his son Solomon was that the Israelites be careful to do all He commanded through Moses. The verse names the laws, statutes and judgments. No battles are listed as a requirement.

Greater, friend. The verse says Manasseh led the people of Judah and Jerusalem astray, so that they did greater evil than the nations the LORD had destroyed before the Israelites. This is a sobering line, and the text says it plainly.

Less would be the easy way to read it, friend, but that's not what the verse says. It says Judah and Jerusalem did greater evil than the nations the LORD had destroyed before the Israelites. Manasseh led them astray, and it shows.
Same would already be bad enough, friend. But the verse goes further. It says the people of Judah and Jerusalem did greater evil than the nations the LORD had destroyed before the Israelites.

That's False, friend. The LORD brings the military commanders of the king of Assyria against them, not Egypt's. Manasseh and his people had been told, and they didn't listen. So the commanders who come are Assyrian.

False is right, friend. The verse says the LORD brought against them the military commanders of the king of Assyria. Egypt isn't in this verse at all. Just a good reminder to read the name on the uniform.

Babylon, friend. It surprised me too, since the commanders serve Assyria's king. But the verse says plainly that they took him to Babylon. I'd have guessed a different city, and I'd have been wrong too.
Nineveh fits an Assyrian king, so I get the guess, friend. But the verse says they took Manasseh to Babylon. That's the one city this verse names.
Damascus is a real city, friend, but it isn't in this verse. The text says the commanders of Assyria's king took Manasseh to Babylon. I'd say that's the city to remember.

Humbles, friend. In his distress, Manasseh seeks the favor of the LORD his God and earnestly humbles himself before the God of his fathers. This is the turning point of his whole story. The man who once built altars in the LORD's house now bows low.

Hiding is a very human move when things go bad, friend. I've ducked behind a cookie rack myself. But this verse says Manasseh earnestly humbled himself before the God of his fathers. He doesn't hide from God here. He comes to Him.

Defending himself would be the opposite of what the verse says, friend. Manasseh sought the favor of the LORD his God and earnestly humbled himself. There's no excuse-making in that line. Just a man coming low.
True, friend. The verse says when Manasseh prayed to Him, the LORD received his plea and heard his petition. After all that Manasseh did, God still hears him. That's worth sitting with for a second.
This one is True, friend. The verse says, “…the LORD received his plea and heard his petition.” Manasseh prays, and the LORD listens. So the statement matches the text.

explanations.answer: Back to Jerusalem and his kingdom
explanations.explanation: Back to Jerusalem and his kingdom, friend. The verse says the LORD brought him back there after receiving his plea. A man in a hook and bronze shackles ends up home on his throne. That's a long way from where he started.
Nineveh is a good guess, since Assyria's commanders took him away, friend. But the verse says the LORD brought him back to Jerusalem and to his kingdom. It's a trip home, not a trip deeper in.

Egypt isn't part of this part of the story, friend. The verse says that after the LORD received his plea, He brought Manasseh back to Jerusalem and to his kingdom. He goes home, not off to a new place.
That the LORD is God, friend. The verse says, “Then Manasseh knew that the LORD is God.” Not a bigger palace or a new crown. The big thing he comes to know is the LORD.

explanations.answer: That his kingdom will last forever
explanations.explanation: That's a bold thing to know, friend, but the verse never says it. It says Manasseh knew that the LORD is God. That's the lesson he comes home with.

explanations.answer: That Assyria will leave him alone
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say a word about Assyria leaving him alone, friend. It says that after the LORD brought him back to Jerusalem, Manasseh knew that the LORD is God. That's the thing he learns.

This one is False, friend. The verse says Manasseh removed the foreign gods and the idol from the house of the LORD. Then he dumped them outside the city. Keeping them in his palace would be like clearing a burnt batch off the tray and sneaking it into a cookie box.

False is right, friend. Manasseh removed the foreign gods and the idol from the house of the LORD, along with the altars he built, and he dumped them outside the city. Nothing goes to his palace. He cleans house, and he means it.

True, friend. After he restored the altar of the LORD and offered peace offerings and thank offerings, he told Judah to serve the LORD, the God of Israel. He had led them astray before. Now he points them the other way.

This one is True, friend. The verse says Manasseh restored the altar of the LORD, sacrificed peace offerings and thank offerings, and told Judah to serve the LORD, the God of Israel. He pointed the people toward the LORD this time.

explanations.answer: Only to the LORD their God
explanations.explanation: Only to the LORD their God, friend. The verse says the people still sacrificed at the high places, “but only to the LORD their God.” So the sacrifices are going to the right One. The high places are still there, and that's what the Nevertheless is pointing at.

explanations.answer: To the Baals of the nations
explanations.explanation: The Baals were part of Manasseh's earlier mess, friend, and I see why you went there. But this verse says the people still sacrificed at the high places, but only to the LORD their God. The Baals aren't mentioned in this one.

explanations.answer: To all the host of heaven
explanations.explanation: Manasseh did worship the host of heaven earlier, friend, but not here. This verse says the people sacrificed at the high places, but only to the LORD their God. That's who the offerings go to.

Two years, friend. Amon, Manasseh's son, reigns in Jerusalem just two years. After his father's fifty-five, that's barely long enough to get comfortable on the throne. It's a short reign and a hard one.
Twelve is a number from this passage, friend, but it belongs to his father. Manasseh was twelve years old when he became king. Amon reigns in Jerusalem two years.
Seven is a nice number, friend, but the verse doesn't use it. Amon, Manasseh's son, reigns in Jerusalem two years. That's far shorter than what you picked.
Increases, friend. The verse says Amon did not humble himself before the LORD as his father Manasseh had done. Instead, he increased his guilt. He had the same chance and went the other direction.
Confessing is what his father Manasseh did when he humbled himself, friend. But this verse is about Amon, and it says he did not humble himself. Instead, he increased his guilt.
Lessening his guilt would've been a good turn, friend, but it's not what the verse says. Amon did not humble himself as his father Manasseh had done. Instead, he increased his guilt.
His son Josiah, friend. The people of the land make Josiah king in Amon's place. Amon's story ends hard, and a new king steps in. I'd say that story isn't over.

Isaiah is a prophet, a man who speaks for God, friend, but he isn't named in this passage. The verse says the people of the land made Amon's son Josiah king in his place. The throne stays in the family.
Hilkiah is a priest, friend, and a priest isn't the one on the throne here. This passage never names him. The people of the land make Amon's son Josiah king in his place.
